title: The wolf and the lamb (Isaiah 11:6–9)
hookLine: the wolf dwells with the lamb, "and a little child shall lead them"

lines: WHO LIES DOWN WITH THE LAMB?
A SHOOT FROM THE STOCK OF JESSE.
cards: Quick question: what lies down with the lamb? A familiar picture is the lion and the lamb, on greeting cards and paintings. But open Isaiah 11 and the lion isn't the one beside the lamb.
The verse is stranger, and more crowded, than the greeting card. It starts with a tree: "And there shall come forth a shoot out of the stock of Jesse, And a twig shall grow forth out of his roots."
From the family of Jesse, King David's father, a new shoot.

teach.h: A KING WHO JUDGES THE POOR.
teach.b: Isaiah describes a coming king from David's line, filled with a spirit of wisdom and understanding, who judges the poor with righteousness. Then the picture widens from the palace to all of creation.
"And the wolf shall dwell with the lamb, And the leopard shall lie down with the kid; And the calf and the young lion and the fatling together; And a little child shall lead them."
The leopard lies down with the young goat. The lion is there too, and the next verse says it shall eat straw like the ox.
Hunter after hunter is set beside its prey. And who's in charge of this strange herd? Not a king, not a soldier: a small child.
A nursing baby plays by the hole of a snake.

teach.h: A LITTLE CHILD SHALL LEAD THEM.
teach.b: Then the reason: "They shall not hurt nor destroy In all My holy mountain; For the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the LORD, As the waters cover the sea."
Jewish tradition reads this as a picture of the messianic age. But how literally?

Maimonides, the medieval teacher, wrote that the world will keep its natural order, and that the wolf and the lamb are a parable: Israel will dwell in safety among nations that once threatened it like wolves and leopards.

teach.h: AS THE WATERS COVER THE SEA.
teach.b: Other readers take the animals more literally. Either way, the ones who were dangerous to each other become neighbors, and the one leading them is a small, trusting child. Strength doesn't make the peace here.
Knowledge of God does, filling the earth like water fills the sea.

how: Jews read Isaiah 11 as a vision of the messianic age; it is read as the haftarah on the last day of Passover outside Israel.

o: a mountain where wild animals hide from hunters
where, in Isaiah's vision, nothing will hurt or destroy
the peak where Elijah faced the prophets of Baal

games.q: the wolf and the lamb — tap the pairs.

s: Isaiah says the lion shall lie down with the lamb
the wolf dwells with the lamb; the lion eats straw like the ox.
in the vision a little child leads the animals
and a little child shall lead them.
Maimonides read the wolf and the lamb as a parable
he wrote that nature keeps its order, and the animals picture Israel living safely among nations that once threatened it.

games.q: you're painting Isaiah's vision. a wolf, a lamb, a leopard, a young goat and a lion are together. who do you paint leading them?
games.why: a little child shall lead them: the small and trusting one is at the front.

practice: Think of two people who don't get along, or two parts of your own life that keep clashing, and picture them side by side, like the wolf and the lamb, with no one getting hurt.
What small, childlike thing would help them dwell together: a shared meal, a joke, an honest question? If you pray, you can ask for peace between them.

wordCard.voice: Holy mountain. The mountain in Isaiah's vision where the wolf lies with the lamb and nothing hurts or destroys, led by a little child. Today's word.
